body.statement: In the balanced six-unit margin instance and for every feasible positive \(r\), let \(X\) be Bernoulli with mean \(1/2\). The compatible coupling that sets \(t(z)=X\) on both \(\mathcal S_1\) and \(\mathcal S_2\), and the compatible coupling that sets \(t(z)=X\) on \(\mathcal S_1\) and \(t(z)=1-X\) on \(\mathcal S_2\), generate covariance matrices with the same first two diagonal entries and respective \((1,2)\) entries \(-1/4\) and \(1/4\); hence neither matrix dominates the other in Loewner order. There is no single matrix \(Q\) that both dominates \(\mathfrak S(r;f,1/2)\) and satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}Qc=\sup_{\Omega\in\mathfrak S(r;f,1/2)}c^{\mathsf T}\Omega c\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^K\). Thus no single conservative quadratic covariance envelope represents the full sharp covariance image or its direction-dependent support function. This separates identification and allocation over the full image from the Harshaw--Middleton--Sävje problem of selecting an admissible estimable quadratic upper bound for a fixed design and estimator.
body.justification: The explicit incomparable pair proves that a sharp covariance-set design is not a relabeling of optimized conservative variance-bound selection.
body.gap: HarshawMiddletonSavje2026 characterizes and optimizes admissible conservative quadratic upper bounds for a fixed design and estimator; this theorem proves non-representability of the compatible covariance image by any one such covariance envelope and retains allocation as a decision variable.
body.consumer: A trial planner learns when a single optimized conservative variance matrix necessarily loses direction-specific information needed to compare several saturation policies.
